items.text: The atoms in the Periodic Table from sodium to argon fill the third shell in exactly the same way, and potassium and calcium start to fill the fourth shell.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATIONS AND THE PERIODIC TABLE

items.label: text
items.text: The electronic configurations of the first 20 elements in the Periodic Table are shown in Figure 4.7.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 4.7 The electronic configurations of the first 20 elements in the Periodic Table

items.label: list_item
items.text: Elements in the same group in the Periodic Table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The number of electrons in the outer shell is the same as the group number for Groups 1 to 7.

items.label: text
items.text: So if you know that barium is in Group 2, you know it has 2 electrons in its outer shell, the same as all the other elements in Group 2. lodine (Group 7) has 7 electrons in its outer shell. Lead (Group 4) has 4 electrons in its outer shell. Working out what is in their inner shells is much more difficult - the simple patterns we have described don't work beyond calcium.

items.label: section_header
items.text: The period number gives the number of occupied shells or the highest occupied shell.

items.label: text
items.text: So, calcium (electronic configuration = 2, 8, 8, 2) is in Period 4 and has four shells occupied; the outermost electron is in the fourth shell. lodine is in Period 5 and has five occupied shells, and because it is also in Group 7 we can deduce that it has7 electrons in the fifth shell.
